narrative:
The model estimated a 90.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In this admission process, that very high predicted risk is why your application was rejected: the school treated it as a signal that you were unlikely to pass the licensing exam, not as a judgment about your character.

The strongest factor was your third-year class-rank decile. Your value was 1, while accepted students averaged roughly 6; this was the single largest push toward the failure prediction. The next most influential factor was your LSAT score of 25.50, well below the accepted-student average of 37.18, and it also pushed strongly toward failure. Your first-year decile was the third most important factor; at 1 versus an accepted average near 6, it added further risk. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.00 was slightly below the accepted average of 3.23, though it was not among the top three drivers. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction.

To improve your chances, focus first on the LSAT: a substantially higher score would directly reduce a major academic concern. Ask an admissions or bar-readiness advisor what specific academic support and evidence they would accept, and consider retaking the LSAT, strengthening your academic record if possible, or reapplying after demonstrating improved readiness. If you believe any record is inaccurate, request correction or appeal.
